title: Analysis of factors influencing injuries and performance in trail running
authors: Soppelsa D, Terrier A, Eghbali P, Traverso A, Dietrich G, Vauclair F, Gremeaux V
population: Trail runners answering a 65-question online survey (97 variables), May 2019 to May 2020; 468 of 697 men.
findings: 697 trail runners (468 men) were included; sixteen injury types reported.
Injury risk was higher with higher weight, fewer interval trainings, lower weekly training volume, lower yearly elevation gain, less regular passive recovery and less sleep.
Number of previous injuries did not affect the risk of a current injury.
Performance increased with training, passive recovery and sleep; it decreased with age, weight and height.
Authors state there might be an upper limit where some of these variables become detrimental, and that more research is needed to find the threshold.
limitations: Self-reported survey, causal Bayesian networks on cross-sectional data, no long-run or back-to-back variable in the abstract, unknown threshold.
implications: No support for a rule that more weekly volume or climbing raises injury risk in this sample; low volume was the risk factor, so a volume floor is more defensible than a tight cap.
The long run is not isolated, so it gives no evidence for the 180/240/270 min feasibility numbers or the 6 h cap.
